title: TransferTraj: A Vehicle Trajectory Learning Model for Region and Task Trans

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract says 'It achieves an average improvement of 83.70% and 33.68% in zero-shot region transferability.' Section 5.1 states these two numbers are TP-task improvements in zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively: 'on the TP task, our method achieves improvements of 83.70% and 33.68% over SOTA models in zero-shot and few-shot settings.' Therefore the abstract mischaracterizes a few-shot result as zero-shot and overgeneralizes task-specific TP numbers to all region transfer.

t2vec is cited as [9], but reference [9] is Fang et al., 'Spatio-temporal trajectory similarity learning in road networks.' The actual t2vec paper is Li et al., 'Deep representation learning for trajectory similarity computation,' which is reference [18] in the bibliography. This misattributes t2vec.

Appendix B.2 says 'L = 2 layers with 128 hidden state dimensions' but Appendix F states 'The optimal value for d is 256; smaller values limit the model's learning capability.' The paper does not clarify whether the main experiments used 128 or 256, and the reported optimal value contradicts the stated setting.

Table 6 reports the full TransferTraj TP RMSE as 197.91 and TP MAE as 144.53. Table 1 on Chengdu reports TransferTraj TP RMSE as 187.91 and MAE as 144.53. The other Table 6 values (TR RMSE 135.15, OD TTE RMSE 2.861) exactly match the Chengdu results in Tables 2 and 3, so the ablation table is for Chengdu; the TP RMSE of 197.91 is internally inconsistent.

Section 4.2 says a fully masked point p_[m]=([m],[m],[m],[m]) has 'masked modalities ... recovered' and pre-training requires points to be 'fully recovered'. However, the Trajectory Modality Predictor in Section 4.1.4 predicts only spatial and temporal modalities (Eq. 5 defines only L^s and L^t). POI and road-network modalities are never generated, so a fully masked point cannot be fully recovered.

Section 4.2 describes pre-training with one randomly selected continuous sub-trajectory from s to e that is fully masked. Appendix B.2 instead says each trajectory is randomly divided into multiple non-overlapping segments and 40% of those segments are selected for trajectory-point masking. These are two different masking protocols and the discrepancy is not explained.

The text says 'we apply the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function' to the predicted modalities, but the temporal loss is written as ||\hat{t}_i - t_i||_2, which is an L2 norm (not squared, not mean). The description of the loss does not match the formula.

The paper justifies omitting zero-shot TR experiments by 'class space inconsistency issues ... where varying road IDs prohibit direct cross-region transfer experiments.' But Appendix B.4 says the TR baselines MTrajRec and RNTrajRec were modified to predict latitude/longitude instead of road IDs, and TransferTraj itself predicts coordinates. Thus road IDs do not prevent zero-shot coordinate-based trajectory recovery evaluation; the stated reason is inconsistent with the actual setup.

The abstract and problem definition state the model can transfer 'without retraining' and 'without needing to retrain the parameters θ'. However, the experimental protocol includes task-specific fine-tuning, and Tables 1-3 present a fine-tuned TransferTraj variant as the best model. Section 5.1 says 'fine-tuning the model and prediction modules consistently yields superior results,' so the 'without retraining' claim is overstated unless explicitly restricted to the zero-shot (wo ft) variant.

The task-definition paragraph contains an extraneous caveat: 'The TR task evaluates recovery under different sparsity ratios, but performance variations are sensitive to local movement complexity and sampling noise. Denser sampling generally aids recovery, though noisy GPS and data heterogeneity can offset gains.' This is not a task protocol and interrupts the definition of the TR input/output; it appears to be a misplaced analytical/hedging remark.
